integration_questions: With the wider ±0.075 m span and seven sensors, does the signal stay linear, or do the outer sensors saturate or drop out on the sharpest slalom bends?
Does the narrower 0.10 m track make the robot oscillate or overshoot at base speeds that keep progress high, and which kp and kd range was stable?
Did the forward lead of 0.07 m cause any phase lag or delayed steering, or did it help anticipate bends?
At which track position does max_error peak, and does line loss occur at the same point?
Which sensors carry most of the signal, and could the outer sensors be given smaller weights?
feedback_request.requested_format: Brief notes on each question, plus the single geometry change you would make first if you could change only one thing.

intent: Test whether a wider sensor span, a narrower wheel track and a lower mass together reduce off-track excursions on bends. Expect the s-bend completion rate to rise above 25 percent and the slalom to complete at least some runs. Expect max_error to fall below 0.06 m and line_loss_events to fall below 1.0 per run on the slalom. Keep the 16 mm footprint, which gave the best score so far, and keep wheel radius and body size fixed.
learning: Iteration 1 showed that the largest gains came from sensing breadth and turning authority, not from average error. Hypotheses to test: (1) a span of ±0.075 m reduces line loss on the slalom; (2) a 0.10 m wheel track improves sharp-bend completion but may increase oscillation; (3) 0.5 kg mass reduces the time to correct large errors. Measurements to request: completion, progress, completion_time, max_error, rms_error, line_loss_events, steering_oscillation and control_effort on each development track.
rationale: Iteration 1 scored 482.7 (up from 64.3). The oval finished 20 of 20 runs. The s-bend finished 5 of 20, and the slalom finished 0 of 20 with progress of only 0.17 and one line-loss event per run. Every failure is an off-track end, with max_error at or above the 0.06 m limit, while rms_error stays small (0.023 to 0.030 m). So the problem is occasional large excursions on bends, not steady tracking error. Body width cannot widen the off-track limit, since max(0.06, 0.0125 + width/4) stays at 0.06 m for every allowed width, so the remaining levers are sensing and drivetrain. Three changes follow from the evidence. (1) The sensors span ±0.06 m, and the line leaves their coverage on the slalom, so I widen the span to ±0.075 m with seven sensors at 0.025 m spacing. (2) Turn rate scales as wheel speed difference divided by wheel_track, so a narrower track gives more yaw per PWM unit. I reduce wheel_track from 0.12 to 0.10 m to recover sharp-bend authority. (3) I move the sensors further ahead (y = 0.07 m) to give the controller more lead time before a bend, and drop mass to 0.5 kg to cut yaw inertia. I keep the 16 mm footprint, which gave the best result so far, along with the wheel radius and body size, so the change in each run stays attributable. Expected result: fewer line-loss events on the slalom and s-bend, max_error below 0.06 m on the bends, and more completions on the s-bend and first completions on the slalom. Main risks: the narrower track may increase oscillation at speed, and a wider span gives each sensor a weaker share of the signal, so the Integrator should check the weights.
